evidence.quote: For I feel like an experiment, I feel exactly like an experiment; it would be impossible for a person to feel more like an experiment than I do, and so I am coming to feel convinced that that is what I AM--an experiment; just an experiment, and nothing more.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator reflects on her own nature and concludes she is an experiment.

evidence.quote: I am almost a whole day old, now.  I arrived yesterday.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator describes having just come into existence a day ago.

evidence.quote: In the rush of finishing up yesterday, the mountains were left in a ragged condition, and some of the plains were so cluttered with rubbish and remnants that the aspects were quite distressing.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator describes a newly created world still being finished and tidied.

evidence.quote: The moon got loose last night, and slid down and fell out of the scheme--a very great loss
evidence.paraphrase: The moon is described as coming loose and falling out of its place in the sky.

evidence.quote: When they first showed, last night, I tried to knock some down with a pole, but it didn't reach, which astonished me; then I tried clods till I was all tired out, but I never got one.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator attempts to reach the stars physically and learns they are unreachable.

evidence.quote: I learned a lesson; also I made an axiom, all out of my own head--my very first one; THE SCRATCHED EXPERIMENT SHUNS THE THORN.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator forms a generalized rule from her experience with thorns.

evidence.quote: I followed the other Experiment around, yesterday afternoon, at a distance, to see what it might be for, if I could.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator observes another creature to determine its purpose.

evidence.quote: It has no hips; it tapers like a carrot; when it stands, it spreads itself apart like a derrick; so I think it is a reptile, though it may be architecture.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator's naive classification of a man as possibly a reptile contrasts with the reader's knowledge.

evidence.quote: It gave me a thrill, for it was the first time I had ever heard speech, except my own.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator is thrilled to hear another being speak for the first time.

evidence.quote: I had created something that didn't exist before; I had added a new thing to the world's uncountable properties
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator recognizes she has introduced fire, a new thing, into the world.

evidence.quote: I laid a dry stick on the ground and tried to bore a hole in it with another one, in order to carry out a scheme that I had
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator experiments by boring a hole to produce an effect.

evidence.quote: I was curious to know what the pink dust was.  Suddenly the name of it occurred to me, though I had never heard of it before.  It was FIRE!
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator identifies and names the newly produced substance as fire.

evidence.quote: FEAR.  And it is horrible!--I wish I had never discovered it; it gives me dark moments, it spoils my happiness, it makes me shiver and tremble and shudder.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator describes discovering and being distressed by the new emotion of fear.

evidence.quote: It is best to prove things by actual experiment; then you KNOW; whereas if you depend on guessing and supposing and conjecturing, you never get educated.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator articulates a method of proving things by experiment rather than conjecture.

evidence.quote: By experiment I know that wood swims, and dry leaves, and feathers, and plenty of other things; therefore by all that cumulative evidence you know that a rock will swim
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator reasons by cumulative evidence from experiments, drawing a faulty conclusion.

evidence.quote: I have experimented and experimented until now I know it never does run uphill, except in the dark.  I know it does in the dark, because the pool never goes dry
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator's mistaken reasoning about water running uphill contrasts with reader knowledge.

evidence.quote: I have seen some of the best ones melt and run down the sky. Since one can melt, they can all melt
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator's belief that stars melt contrasts with the reader's understanding of stars.

evidence.quote: When the mighty brontosaurus came striding into camp, she regarded it as an acquisition, I considered it a calamity
evidence.paraphrase: A brontosaurus appears in the story's world, placing it in a prehistoric or mythical setting.

evidence.quote: When I look back, the Garden is a dream to me.  It was beautiful, surpassingly beautiful, enchantingly beautiful; and now it is lost, and I shall not see it any more.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator describes the loss of the Garden after the Fall.
